why = Callout("warning", "Correctness requirement, not an optimization", "Naively queuing send, edit, delete ops offline leaves edit/delete targeting an id the server has never seen: best case a 404 and failed ops, worst case a ghost message from out-of-order arrival.")
rules = Table([queued, newOp, result])
queued = Col("Queued", ["send", "send", "send", "edit", "edit", "react(add)", "read(ord=5)"])
newOp = Col("New op", ["edit", "delete", "react", "edit", "delete", "react(remove)", "read(ord=9)"])
result = Col("Result", ["Rewrite the send payload with the new body — one op", "Drop both — never touches the network", "Keep both, ordered — the react must follow the send", "Keep the last", "Drop the edit, keep the delete", "Drop both (same emoji + user)", "Keep the higher — max-register"])
note = Text("Not covered by a rule above: reads may drop all but the newest per chat, and blob_upload must complete before the send that references it (§10.3).")
ref = FileRef("docs/DESIGN.md", 1848, "§10.4 Outbox coalescing")

reply:
The rules live in §10.4 (`docs/DESIGN.md:1848`). Coalescing runs **on enqueue**, is scoped by `target_id`, and is a correctness requirement — without it, an offline compose → edit → delete queues ops against a message id the server has never seen.

Two things worth noting beyond the table:

- **The `react` key includes the actor**, so toggling the same emoji only cancels when it's the same user — different users' reactions can never coalesce.
- The doc warns to implement this **early**: retrofitting means auditing every op kind against every other, "a combinatorial review nobody enjoys."
